title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning
authors: Xiangyu Sun, Shirin Hosseinmardi, Ramin Bostanabad
abstract: Large-scale topology optimization (TO) remains computationally demanding, especially for stress-constrained problems. To address this challenge, we propose the simultaneous neural topology optimization (SNTO) framework where we represent state, adjoint, and design variables with custom neural networks (NNs) whose parameters are jointly optimized within a single optimization loop that leverages continuous adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation. This optimization minimizes a multi-component loss function that combines the design objective, an aggregation of the local stress constraints, and the potential energy functionals. Our NNs have a unique architecture that accelerates convergence while enabling the networks to capture sharp gradients and boundaries which are critical to stress-constrained TO. To achieve scalability to millions of degrees of freedom (DoF), we develop a hardware-aware training scheme in which the design domain is partitioned into subdomains that are distributed across multiple GPUs. To control peak GPU memory usage, we further slice each subdomain into smaller regions whose loss gradients are evaluated sequentially and accumulated to update the NN parameters. Unlike domain decomposition approaches, our partitioning naturally ensures field continuity across the subdomains and does not require the introduction of additional terms into the loss function. For validation, we first evaluate the proposed framework on various 2D stress-constrained benchmarks and compare our results to a conventional finite element-based approach, showing that SNTO produces super-resolution designs with sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions. We then consider large-scale 3D problems with up to eight million collocation points and distribute the training over up to eight GPUs.

infographic.key_insight: Simultaneous neural topology optimization jointly optimizes state, adjoint, and design networks to produce high-resolution stress-constrained designs while scaling across GPUs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets lower-material structural designs under stress limits while addressing the computational demands of large-scale topology optimization.
method: Jointly train custom neural networks using continuous adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation.
Combine the design objective, aggregated local stress constraints, and potential energy functionals in one loss.
Distribute spatial partitions across GPUs and accumulate gradients over smaller slices to control peak memory without additional interface-loss terms.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 2D benchmarks, SNTO produced sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions than a conventional finite element-based approach; 3D demonstrations reached eight million collocation points on up to eight GPUs.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify runtime savings or local stress-constraint violations, leaving computational efficiency and constraint fidelity to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning

title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: For shape-informed hemodynamic surrogates, active learning and finite-element physical consistency are more effective during fine-tuning than during early or full-training use.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports scalable, patient-specific prediction of aortic velocity and pressure fields at peak systole across varying vascular anatomies.
method: Generate physiologically consistent CFD data from SynthAorta geometries using automatic boundary-condition adjustment.
Represent anatomies as displacement fields from a common reference and train Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogates.
Explore gradient- and subspace-based active learning alongside differentiable finite-element residual constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved fine-tuning performance from active learning and physical consistency constraints, while out-of-distribution tests identify geometric parametrization support as the main limitation; no quantitative metrics are provided.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to unfamiliar anatomies depends on the geometric coverage of the underlying parametrization, not just the network architecture.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers
authors: Zumrat Usmanova, Ruobing Bai
abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that rotating the director costs no free energy. The corresponding neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.

infographic.key_insight: Ideal liquid crystal elastomers couple mesogen orientation with network deformation, enabling reversible actuation and soft deformation through continuously connected stress-free states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory provides a constitutive foundation for modeling LCE actuators and compliant structures with programmable shape changes and low-stress deformation.
method: Connect anisotropic Gaussian-chain statistics to neo-classical continuum elasticity.
Explain spontaneous deformation and stripe-domain soft elasticity through non-quasi-convex free energy.
Use quasi-convex relaxation to classify three macroscopic response phases in polydomain LCEs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a theoretical review and phase classification, without reporting experimental datasets or quantitative validation.
infographic.watch_item: Ideal soft elasticity assumes no crosslinking-state memory; practical simulations may require network nonideality, director-gradient elasticity, and rate-dependent effects.
infographic.paper_title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers

title: A high-order multi-scale method and its error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems in composite materials
authors: Gehao Wang, Hao Dong, Yufeng Nie, Junzhi Cui
abstract: Significant spatial heterogeneity and nonlocal history-dependent attenuation jointly govern wave propagation in composite materials, making full-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) computationally prohibitive. This study proposed a high-order multi-scale (HOMS) method for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems with highly oscillatory and discontinuous material coefficients. Using a multi-scale asymptotic expansion approach, the macroscopic homogenized equation, and first- and second-order correction terms are derived to construct the high-accuracy HOMS solution. Moreover, a local pointwise error analysis identifies the leading residual eliminated by this HOMS solution and validates its local physical balance preservation. Then, a global energy-norm error estimate establishes the $O(\varepsilon)$-order convergence rate for the HOMS solution. Subsequently, an efficient spatiotemporal multi-scale algorithm integrating the finite element and finite difference methods is designed, which employs a novel fully discrete $L2\text{-}1_σ$-Newmark scheme, and corresponding unconditional shifted-energy stability and explicit convergence rates are also obtained for the macroscopic homogenized displacement and velocity, respectively. Both two- and three-dimensional examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, reduced cost, and robustness of the proposed HOMS method. This work provides an effective multi-scale tool for nonlocal-in-time wave simulation in engineering applications.

infographic.key_insight: A high-order multiscale method captures heterogeneous, fractionally damped wave propagation with a proven O(ε) global energy-norm error bound.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method reduces the cost of simulating waves in composite materials with fine-scale heterogeneity and history-dependent attenuation.
method: Derive a homogenized wave equation with first- and second-order multiscale corrections.
Combine finite elements with an L2-1σ–Newmark time-discretization scheme.
Establish local residual cancellation, global error bounds, and unconditional shifted-energy stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two- and three-dimensional numerical examples demonstrate accuracy, efficiency, reduced computational cost, and robustness; the abstract reports no numerical speedup factors.
infographic.watch_item: Fractional damping requires temporal history treatment, so memory and runtime costs should be assessed for long-duration simulations.
infographic.paper_title: A high-order multi-scale method and its error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems in composite materials

title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?
authors: Pratik Worah, Randall Bateman
abstract: Progressive neuronal loss is the hallmark of neurodegenerative disease, yet how loss of neurons shapes the pattern of cognitive decline remains poorly understood. Here we systematically ablate neurons (computational units) in language models spanning recurrent long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer architectures and apply limited fine-tuning as a simple proxy for compensatory plasticity. With whole-unit ablation, LSTMs degrade gradually with syntactic and semantic faculties declining in parallel across mild-to-moderate damage. By contrast, Transformers exhibit late threshold-like collapse under feedforward multi-layer perceptron (MLP) ablation and smoother sigmoid-like decline under attention-head ablation. Qualitatively, MLP-ablated models continue to make within-category semantic substitutions (semantic paraphasias) alongside rising non-responses, paralleling Wernicke-type aphasia, while attention-head ablation produces a trend toward loss of semantic specificity similar to the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (svPPA). These findings indicate that feedforward and attentional pathways have functionally distinct failure modes, suggesting that architecture-dependent failure profiles may offer new computational perspectives on aphasic syndromes and neurodegenerative diseases as an in silico model. Notably, early accuracy retention under Transformer attention-head ablation qualitatively parallels pre-symptomatic reserve before the 40--60% neuronal loss reported by Gomez-Isla et al. (1996) when clinical symptoms emerge in Alzheimer's disease, whereas the steadier LSTM decline parallels the symptomatic progression described by DeKosky and Scheff (1990) and Terry et al. (1991).

infographic.key_insight: Neuron ablation produces architecture-dependent language failures: gradual decline in LSTMs, threshold-like collapse under Transformer MLP ablation, and smoother sigmoid-like decline under attention-head ablation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These distinct damage-response profiles can inform robustness testing of AI systems, though the study does not directly evaluate solid-mechanics applications.
method: Systematically ablate computational units in LSTM and Transformer language models.
Apply limited fine-tuning as a proxy for compensatory plasticity.
Compare language degradation under whole-unit, MLP, and attention-head ablation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parallel syntactic and semantic decline in LSTMs, semantic substitutions and rising non-responses after MLP ablation, and reduced semantic specificity after attention-head ablation.
infographic.watch_item: Similarities to aphasia are qualitative; computational ablation and limited fine-tuning do not establish biological equivalence to neuronal loss and recovery.
infographic.paper_title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?

title: Mixed finite element methods for a heat-assisted model of sedimentation
authors: Julio Careaga, Cristian Inzunza
abstract: A model for the consolidation-sedimentation process incorporating thermal effects is analysed. The model is motivated by novel applications to heat-assisted sedimentation of mineral suspensions. A system of convection-diffusion equations for the concentration and temperature are coupled to flow equations for the volume-average velocity and pressure. The model is supplemented with Dirichlet and mixed boundary conditions. A quasi-stationary approach of the system is analysed by means of a mixed variational formulation, where additional variables such as the pseudostress tensor and variables for the gradient of the temperature and concentration are introduced. The existence and uniqueness of the system is shown making use of the Babu{\v s}ka-Brezzi theory and Banach's fixed-point theorem, under hypotheses of smallness of the data and additional regularity on the solutions. A discrete formulation based on finite element spaces is proposed and analysed, and the existence of solutions is achieved thanks to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. Additionally, Céa and a priori estimates are derived for the mixed formulation. Finally, numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the performance of the model and to confirm the theoretical rates of convergence.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed finite element framework couples sediment concentration, temperature, velocity, and pressure to model heat-assisted consolidation–sedimentation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports simulation of thermally assisted settling of mineral suspensions, accounting for interactions between heat transport and sedimentation.
method: Formulate the quasi-stationary coupled system using pseudostress and concentration and temperature gradient variables.
Establish continuous well-posedness via Babuška–Brezzi theory and Banach’s fixed-point theorem under stated assumptions.
Analyze a mixed finite element discretization using Brouwer’s theorem and derive Céa-type and a priori error estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples demonstrate model performance and confirm theoretical convergence rates; the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Continuous existence and uniqueness require small-data and additional solution-regularity assumptions, limiting guarantees outside those conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Mixed finite element methods for a heat-assisted model of sedimentation

title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
authors: Reza T Batley, Sourav Saha
abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.

infographic.key_insight: Rectified-flow generation paired with exact latent-space refinement enables concurrent design of printable scaffold microstructures and their spatial placement to meet whole-bone mechanical targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports highly porous bone scaffolds that preserve target mechanical responses while enforcing feature-size constraints.
method: Generate periodic lattice cells with a conditional rectified-flow model.
Refine cells in latent space using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities.
Jointly optimize cell geometry and spatial assignment under mechanical and feature-size constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Computational benchmarks report under 1% error across six prescribed moduli for all eight rabbit-case refinements, plus human femoral scaffolds with 63% and 84% porosity meeting reported compliance or strain-energy targets.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational validation; physical printability, fatigue performance, and biological integration remain to be demonstrated experimentally.
infographic.paper_title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement

title: Sparse-grid discretizations of BGG sequences
authors: Yihanqi Hu, Yuwen Li
abstract: We develop the first tensor-product sparse-grid finite element discretizations of Bernstein--Gelfand--Gelfand (BGG) complexes. Alpert wavelets and their first and second primitives yield compatible hierarchies of discontinuous, continuous, and continuously differentiable piecewise polynomials, that serve as one-dimensional ingredients of BGG sparse-grid finite elements. We construct a bounded commuting sparse-grid projection that yields stable discrete potentials for Hessian, elasticity, and div-div complexes. Under mixed Sobolev regularity, we prove sparse-grid approximation estimates with dimension-independent convergence rates in the number of degrees of freedom. Experiments for a three-dimensional incompatibility problem and a two-dimensional biharmonic problem on an annulus illustrate the efficiency of sparse grids relative to full grids.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces tensor-product sparse-grid finite elements for BGG complexes, with dimension-independent convergence rates in degrees of freedom under mixed Sobolev regularity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These structure-preserving discretizations can reduce computational cost for elasticity-related and higher-order mechanics problems while retaining stable discrete potentials.
method: Build compatible polynomial hierarchies from Alpert wavelets and their first and second primitives.
Construct sparse-grid BGG finite elements for Hessian, elasticity, and div-div complexes.
Establish a bounded commuting projection and sparse-grid approximation estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a 3D incompatibility problem and a 2D biharmonic problem on an annulus illustrate efficiency relative to full grids.
infographic.watch_item: The convergence guarantees require mixed Sobolev regularity, which should be checked for problems with singularities or limited solution smoothness.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse-grid discretizations of BGG sequences

title: Inverse domain uncertainty quantification in hemodynamics: sampling virtual patient cohorts under constraints
authors: Francesco Romor, Jose Rodrigo Rojo-Garcia, André-Alexander Zepernick, Ana Djurdjevac, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: We consider the following inverse domain uncertainty quantification problem: given a prescribed value or measurement of a hemodynamic biomarker, characterize the distribution of vascular geometries compatible with it. The problem is formulated as a Bayesian inverse problem in which a high-dimensional latent parameter encodes the cardiovascular shape and accounts for inter-patient variability. The parameter-to-observable map composes a conditional LDDMM stochastic interpolant generating the aortic surface with a high-performance numerical finite element solver for the unsteady incompressible Navier--Stokes equations, from which biomarkers of interest are evaluated. The map is nonlinear, high-dimensional and computationally expensive. To address the problem, we compare three ensemble strategies: ensemble adjusted Kalman inversion (EAKI), adaptive Bayesian updating with structural reliability (aBUS), and a Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao (WFR) sequential Monte Carlo scheme. The first two approaches are derivative-free. For the third method, we introduce a novel differentiable flow-matching surrogate that reduces the cost of a single forward map evaluation at the price of a distribution shift depending on the training distribution used for the surrogate. We apply the framework to the generation of virtual patient cohorts matching prescribed pressure drops along aortic geometries affected by coarctation, and we validate and compare the three methods on synthetic data.

infographic.key_insight: Bayesian inverse modeling generates virtual aortic patient cohorts whose geometries are compatible with prescribed hemodynamic biomarkers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty-aware cardiovascular simulation by identifying multiple plausible anatomies consistent with a target pressure drop.
method: Encode vascular shape in a high-dimensional latent space using a conditional LDDMM stochastic interpolant.
Evaluate biomarkers with an unsteady incompressible Navier–Stokes finite element solver.
Compare EAKI, aBUS, and WFR sequential Monte Carlo, introducing a differentiable flow-matching surrogate for WFR.
infographic.evidence_signal: The three methods are validated and compared on synthetic data for aortic coarctation cohorts matching prescribed pressure drops.
infographic.watch_item: The surrogate reduces forward-evaluation cost but introduces distribution shift that depends on its training distribution.
infographic.paper_title: Inverse domain uncertainty quantification in hemodynamics: sampling virtual patient cohorts under constraints

title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images
authors: Jihoon Kim, Yongmin Kwon, Namwoo Kang
abstract: Deep generative design can produce complex geometries, but unconstrained representations may create undercuts that prevent release from a two-part mold. We present CAST, which reformulates three-dimensional shape generation under a selected mold-opening constraint as a two-dimensional image generation problem using paired top and bottom depth images. Each valid depth pair defines one material interval along a selected mold-opening direction, so reconstructions exclude undercuts in that direction by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and a finite element analysis (FEA) guided optimizer refines the same two boundaries. We evaluate diffusion-based generation with limited training data comprising 211 SimJEB bracket designs. On SimJEB brackets, FEA-guided refinement with a volume penalty reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates. The median reduction across all candidates was 36.8 percent in the optimization FEA model. Reconstruction of existing brackets revealed a mass--stiffness trade-off: filling occluded regions increased material volume and reduced displacement under the evaluated loads. Paired depth images thus connect generative exploration and structural refinement in a shared design space that preserves the selected pull-direction restriction.

infographic.key_insight: CAST uses paired top and bottom depth images to generate and optimize 3D shapes without undercuts along a selected mold-opening direction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared, pull-direction-constrained design space connects generative exploration with FEA-guided structural refinement for two-part-mold designs.
method: Represent geometry as one material interval per ray using paired depth images.
Generate candidate shapes with diffusion models trained on bracket designs.
Refine both depth boundaries using FEA-guided optimization with a volume penalty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 211 SimJEB training designs, FEA-guided refinement reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates, with a 36.8% median reduction across all candidates in the optimization FEA model.
infographic.watch_item: Undercut exclusion applies only to the selected pull direction; it does not establish full casting feasibility.
infographic.paper_title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images

title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning
authors: Yongyi Wu, Zheng Wang, Sen Lin
abstract: Online Continual Learning (OCL) requires models to learn from non-stationary data streams under a strict single-pass constraint, making them highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. While existing studies have explored various strategies from data, architecture, and optimization perspectives, the optimizer often directly uses generic approaches such as SGD and AdamW. In this work, we reveal a new link between optimization dynamics and OCL needs by recasting Polyak-Ruppert averaging as the engine of "plasticity" and Primal averaging as the anchor of "stability". This inspires our novel optimizer, SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation), which explicitly decouples plasticity and stability by interpolating between a fast-moving "plasticity" sequence and an adaptive "stability" sequence. We theoretically demonstrate that SPIN implicitly employs an inverse Hessian approximation, providing crucial Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy, single-sample Hessian estimates and mitigate forgetting. More importantly, SPIN can be seamlessly integrated into existing OCL methods by taking resulted gradients as input and replacing standard optimizers. Extensive experiments show that using SPIN instead of standard optimizers yields consistent and significant performance gains across multiple OCL approaches, including the challenging rehearsal-free setting and under strict memory constraints.

infographic.key_insight: SPIN targets catastrophic forgetting in online continual learning by interpolating between fast plasticity and adaptive stability sequences.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPIN could support models adapting to evolving engineering data streams, though the abstract reports no solid-mechanics-specific validation.
method: Connect Polyak–Ruppert averaging to plasticity and primal averaging to stability.
Interpolate the two sequences to balance new learning and retained knowledge.
Replace standard optimizers using existing gradients, with an implicit regularized inverse-Hessian approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent performance gains across multiple online continual learning approaches, including rehearsal-free learning and strict memory constraints, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Hyperparameter sensitivity and computational overhead should be checked before deployment; neither is quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning

title: A hybridization-derived interior penalty Nitsche method for heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion
authors: Vincent Fontaine
abstract: We develop an interior penalty Nitsche finite element formulation for heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion problems, which is derived from an interior-penalty stabilized Lagrange multiplier method. A distinctive feature of the derived method is that it simultaneously combines two popular stabilization strategies: (i) a boundary penalty mechanism similar to Nitsche's methods and (ii) an interior penalty mechanism as for Continuous Interior Penalty (CIP) methods. Furthermore, the normal component of the numerical flux is single-valued across the mesh skeleton and available in closed form. We establish the equivalence between the hybridized Lagrange multiplier formulation and its condensed Interior Penalty Nitsche (IPN) form, and we deliver the stability and convergence analysis of the latter. For sufficiently regular solutions, we establish energy-norm error estimates for the three symmetry variants. Under a piecewise elliptic regularity assumption on the adjoint problem, the $L^2$ estimate is optimal for the symmetric variant and exhibits a half-order loss for the incomplete and nonsymmetric variants; its constant may depend on the diffusion coefficients through the adjoint regularity constant. This single-valued numerical normal flux, available in closed form, provides a starting point for locally conservative $H(\mathrm{div})$-conforming flux reconstruction, left for future work. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: A hybridization-derived Interior Penalty Nitsche method combines boundary and interior stabilization for heterogeneous, anisotropic diffusion while providing a closed-form, single-valued numerical normal flux.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation supports finite element simulation of diffusion-driven engineering processes with spatially varying and direction-dependent material properties.
method: Derive the formulation from an interior-penalty-stabilized Lagrange multiplier method.
Prove equivalence between the hybridized formulation and its condensed Interior Penalty Nitsche form.
Establish stability and convergence for symmetric, incomplete, and nonsymmetric variants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments validate the theory: under stated regularity assumptions, the symmetric variant achieves optimal L2 convergence, while incomplete and nonsymmetric variants lose half an order.
infographic.watch_item: Locally conservative H(div)-conforming flux reconstruction remains future work; the available numerical normal flux is a starting point, not a completed reconstruction.
infographic.paper_title: A hybridization-derived interior penalty Nitsche method for heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion

title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models
authors: Alessandro Palma, Charles Jones, Tristan Cinquin, Fabian J. Theis, Frederik Wenkel
abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.

infographic.key_insight: Trajectory replay updates continuous-time generative models while preserving prior tasks by matching historical and incoming velocity fields instead of repeatedly generating replay samples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support continual updates of generative engineering surrogates, but the abstract reports no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: Match a frozen historical velocity field along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field.
Balance retention and adaptation with a stability–plasticity coefficient, yielding density-weighted velocity mixing.
Use mean velocity distillation to access historical trajectories with few network evaluations per update.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better class-incremental image generation than generative replay and distillation baselines, plus two biological case studies preserving treatment-effect prediction across new contexts and batches.
infographic.watch_item: Engineering deployment would require validating physical consistency and sensitivity to the stability–plasticity coefficient.
infographic.paper_title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models

title: Learning without Overwriting: Structural Knowledge Fusion for Continual Learning
authors: Kanishk Bakshi, Amitansu Pattanaik, Kathiravan Srinivasan
abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in sequential deep learning arises from a fixed-capacity architectural constraint: parameter updates encoding new tasks perturb weight subspaces supporting prior representations. We introduce the Knowledge Fusion Network (KFN), which mitigates the stability-plasticity trade-off in class-incremental learning through novelty-gated structural expansion rather than parameter negotiation within a shared capacity budget. KFN decouples task acquisition from knowledge consolidation: each incoming task is learned in an isolated lightweight specialist network (2.8M parameters) and integrated into the global model via a Structural Fusion Module that allocates dedicated channel capacity conditioned on a quantitative novelty score. Dual structural isolation--channel-space separation with temporally phased gradient unfreezing--protects consolidated knowledge. On ten-task Split CIFAR-100, KFN achieves 11.94% minimum task accuracy and 71.16% task-10 accuracy, whereas shared-parameter baselines degrade severely: LwF to 9.07% average accuracy (0.00% min), Replay++ to 8.91% (85.08% forgetting), and Replay to 16.21% (73.44% forgetting); KFN's forgetting (57.92%) is 15.5 pp lower than Replay. Furthermore, KFN prevents logit-scale drift, maintaining near-symmetric task performance. Across CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT satellite imagery, KFN's class-incremental retention (72.7% and 42.5%) substantially exceeds the best baselines (29.6% and 0.94%). Crucially, KFN achieves parameter-efficient linear scaling, adding 25% of the base parameter count per step and requiring 25.1% of naive backbone duplication over ten tasks (28.1M vs 112.0M). With a 37.1% peak GPU memory reduction over full retraining, KFN establishes novelty-gated expansion as a practical path beyond fixed-capacity architectures.

infographic.key_insight: Knowledge Fusion Network (KFN) reduces catastrophic forgetting by adding novelty-gated capacity rather than repeatedly overwriting shared parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: KFN could support sequential learning in engineering workflows, but the abstract does not validate constitutive modeling or solid-mechanics applications.
method: Learn each incoming task in an isolated 2.8M-parameter specialist network.
Fuse new knowledge into the global model using dedicated channels allocated by a quantitative novelty score.
Protect consolidated knowledge through channel separation and phased gradient unfreezing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Split CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT, KFN reports class-incremental retention of 72.7% and 42.5%, versus best-baseline values of 29.6% and 0.94%, while using 28.1M parameters versus 112.0M for backbone duplication over ten tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Capacity still grows with task count, and scalability beyond the reported ten-task setting remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Learning without Overwriting: Structural Knowledge Fusion for Continual Learning

title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
authors: Xiaoyin Chen, Yizheng Huang, Yinglun Xu, Ziyun Zhao, Emmett McQuinn, Julie Liu
abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.

infographic.key_insight: Self-evolving agents can improve overall performance without updating model weights, but greater adaptability often comes at the cost of retaining earlier capabilities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational engineering assistants, prompt, memory, or skill updates should be checked for regressions before deployment across changing tools and workflows.
method: Keep model weights frozen while adapting prompts, memory, or skills from task feedback.
Evaluate ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness on four drifting task streams.
Compare adaptation gains with retention and interference across tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four streams built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld, self-evolution improved aggregate performance on most streams, but higher plasticity consistently reduced stability.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no solid-mechanics benchmark; shared edits and conflicting memory retrieval warrant domain-specific regression testing.
infographic.paper_title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?

title: A recovery based linear finite element method for the Monge--Ampère equation
authors: Tianyang Chu, Hailong Guo, Zhimin Zhang
abstract: In this paper, we study finite element approximations of a fourth-order perturbed semilinear partial differential equation that arises naturally in the computation of viscosity solutions to the fully nonlinear Monge--Ampère equation. We develop a novel recovery-based $C^0$ linear finite element method for discretizing this model problem. The key analytical tool is a Miranda--Talenti-type estimate for the recovery operator, which guides the formulation of the discrete scheme and guarantees its well-posedness. We rigorously establish convergence in the $H^2$ norm by employing a fixed-point argument. Furthermore, optimal $H^1$-error estimates are derived using a duality argument. Numerical experiments confirm the efficiency of the proposed method and validate the theoretical convergence results.

infographic.key_insight: A recovery-based C⁰ linear finite element method approximates a fourth-order perturbed PDE used to compute viscosity solutions of the fully nonlinear Monge–Ampère equation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a mathematically supported discretization strategy for nonlinear PDE computation using low-order finite elements, rather than an AI surrogate.
method: Use a recovery operator to construct a C⁰ linear finite element discretization.
Establish well-posedness with a Miranda–Talenti-type estimate and H² convergence through a fixed-point argument.
Derive optimal H¹-error estimates using a duality argument.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments support the method’s efficiency and theoretical convergence results, though the abstract reports no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence is established for the perturbed model; the abstract does not specify how perturbation choices affect accuracy relative to the original Monge–Ampère equation.
infographic.paper_title: A recovery based linear finite element method for the Monge--Ampère equation

title: Deciding Scale Placement in MXFP4 Dot Products with Integer Arithmetic
authors: Shreyas Vinayakumar
abstract: The Open Compute Project's microscaling (MX) family includes MXFP4, which stores 32 four-bit elements with a shared power-of-two scale. When lowering a dot-product reduction, a compiler can apply these scales before the reduction, or defer scaling until afterwards. Although equivalent over real numbers, these formulations can produce different IEEE binary32 results through overflow or underflow, with equivalence also depending on the reduction tree. We study the legality of compiler rewrites in either direction by deriving conditions under which the two formulations are bitwise equivalent. To decide rewrite legality, we construct an integer state machine that exploits the finite element alphabet and shared power-of-two scales, modeling overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding. We prove its faithfulness under bounded scale codes and integer coefficients, yielding an exact encoding of the equivalence query in quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic (QF_LIA). For MXFP4, we derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents for any fixed binary reduction tree within the supported coefficient range. This bound depends on the size of the largest proper subtree. For four tree shapes at block lengths $k\in\{2,3,4,8,16,32\}$ and two shapes at $k=64$, SMT finds counterexamples when this upper bound is increased by one exponent step. Against the standard direct encoding in quantifier-free floating-point arithmetic (QF_FP), on matched queries cvc5 proves the integer version in seconds but reaches a configured one-CPU-hour limit on the floating-point proof even at $k=2$. The implementation was cross-checked using an independent floating-point encoding, exhaustive and stratified binary32 execution, and GPU replay of counterexamples. An MLIR lowering prototype demonstrates selection between the two formulations using the certified conditions as static or runtime guards.

infographic.key_insight: An integer-arithmetic model can certify when moving shared power-of-two scales across an MXFP4 dot-product reduction preserves bitwise binary32 results.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Certified scale placement can support correctness-preserving compiler optimizations for low-precision kernels potentially used in FEM surrogates, though no mechanics application is evaluated.
method: Model overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding with a faithful integer state machine.
Encode rewrite equivalence in QF_LIA and derive a sufficient scale-exponent bound that depends on the reduction tree.
Use certified conditions as static or runtime guards in an MLIR lowering prototype.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across tested reduction trees and block lengths up to 64, SMT found counterexamples one exponent step above the bound; on matched queries, cvc5 proved integer encodings in seconds while direct floating-point proofs hit a one-CPU-hour limit even at length 2.
infographic.watch_item: Certificates depend on bounded scale codes, supported integer coefficients, and the specified reduction tree; changing these assumptions requires renewed validation.
infographic.paper_title: Deciding Scale Placement in MXFP4 Dot Products with Integer Arithmetic

title: Impact of Torque Ripple Induced Angular Oscillations on Maxwell Pressure Harmonics in Permanent-Magnet Synchronous Machines
authors: Thomas Poupon, Arthur Givois, Vincent Lanfranchi, Jean-Daniel Chazot, Tahar Hamiti
abstract: Torque ripple in electrical machines is a wellknown source of noise and vibration. While numerous studies focus on control strategies to mitigate this ripple, the feedback mechanism by which the resulting mechanical oscillations influence the electromagnetic forces remains less explored. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the impact of torque ripple on the rotor angular dynamics and the subsequent generation of new harmonics in the Maxwell pressure distribution. We first develop an analytical model for a rigid rotor subjected to a single torque harmonic, revealing the inherently non-linear nature of the angular response. This analysis demonstrates the creation of new harmonics in the rotor motion and a slight reduction in the mean rotational speed. The study is then extended to a flexible rotor model incorporating torsional modes, solved using the Finite Element Method. Finally, we introduce a strongly coupled magneto-mechanical model, based on the subdomain method, to quantify how these rotor oscillations modulate the air-gap magnetic field. The results show a new modulated spatio-temporal harmonic distribution in the Maxwell pressure spectrum, which is not predicted by conventional uncoupled models. These findings are crucial for high-fidelity Noise, Vibration, and Harshness (NVH) analysis, as these additional pressure waves can excite stator structural modes.

infographic.key_insight: Torque-ripple-induced rotor oscillations feed back into the magnetic field, creating additional Maxwell pressure harmonics missed by conventional uncoupled models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Capturing these additional pressure waves can improve NVH predictions because they may excite stator structural modes.
method: Derive nonlinear rigid-rotor dynamics under a single torque harmonic.
Extend the analysis to a flexible rotor with torsional modes using FEM.
Couple rotor dynamics and subdomain electromagnetics to evaluate air-gap field modulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports model-based findings of new rotor-motion harmonics, a slight mean-speed reduction, and additional spatio-temporal Maxwell pressure harmonics, without quantitative metrics or experimental validation details.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation and the computational cost of strong magneto-mechanical coupling are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Impact of Torque Ripple Induced Angular Oscillations on Maxwell Pressure Harmonics in Permanent-Magnet Synchronous Machines

title: A Novel Two-Level Domain Decomposition Method with Physically Motivated Coarse Space for Surface Acoustic Wave Device Simulations
authors: Likun Qiu, Jianguo Huang, Xuejun Xu
abstract: The surface acoustic wave (SAW) equations are fundamental in describing the operating principle of SAW devices, which are characterized by high operating frequency, multiphysics coupling, and defined on an unbounded domain. Finite element (FE) simulation is one of the most accurate numerical methods for such devices. However, the method usually leads to ill-conditioned linear systems with a large number of degrees of freedom (DOFs), limiting its application. To address this issue, based on the finite element tearing and interconnecting (FETI) algorithm, this paper proposes a domain decomposition method with iteration numbers stable with respect to number of subdomains, frequency and mesh size, named FETI-SAW. The main novelty is that the Dirichlet preconditioner combined with a Rayleigh-wave-based coarse space is constructed to produce a preconditioned iterative algorithm for the Lagrange multiplier linear system. In some sense, this method reflects the physical essence of the SAW equations. In numerical experiments, we take interdigital transducers (IDT) and SAW resonators as examples to demonstrate the efficiency of the FETI-SAW algorithm. Additionally, the MATLAB and C++ source codes accompanying this paper are provided.

infographic.key_insight: FETI-SAW combines a Dirichlet preconditioner with a physically motivated Rayleigh-wave coarse space to stabilize iterative finite element solves for surface acoustic wave devices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets large, ill-conditioned systems arising in high-frequency, coupled-physics SAW device simulations.
method: Decompose the finite element domain using finite element tearing and interconnecting (FETI).
Construct a two-level solver with Dirichlet preconditioning and a Rayleigh-wave-based coarse space.
Iteratively solve the interface Lagrange multiplier system.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on interdigital transducers and SAW resonators demonstrate efficiency, with iteration counts reported as stable across subdomain counts, frequencies, and mesh sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify speedups or coarse-space costs; this is a numerical solver, not a learned FEM surrogate.
infographic.paper_title: A Novel Two-Level Domain Decomposition Method with Physically Motivated Coarse Space for Surface Acoustic Wave Device Simulations

title: Abaqus implementation of the phase-field approach to fracture
authors: Jiangwei Zhou, Victor Lefevre, Oscar Lopez-Pamies
abstract: In this paper, we introduce an Abaqus user-subroutine implementation of the phase-field model of fracture initiated by Kumar, Francfort, and Lopez-Pamies (\emph{J. Mech. Phys. Solids} 112, 523--551, 2018). The implementation is presented for the basic case of isotropic linear elastic brittle materials with a Drucker-Prager strength surface. The material inputs are therefore the Young's modulus $E$, the Poisson's ratio $ν$, the uniaxial tensile strength $\sts$, the uniaxial compressive strength $\scs$, and the fracture toughness $G_c$. The mathematical correspondence between the heat equation and the evolution equation for the phase field $v(\bfX,t)$ is exploited through a UMAT subroutine, wherein the driving force $c_{\texttt{e}}(\bfX,t)$ --- accounting for the material strength surface --- in the phase-field model plays the role of a heat source. To ensure that the equations for the displacement field $\bfu(\bfX,t)$ and the phase field $v(\bfX,t)$ are solved in a staggered manner --- a solution strategy that, as opposed to monolithic approaches, reliably yields the correct physical solution --- we make use of a combination of UEXTERNALDB, UAMP, MPC, and URDFIL subroutines. Within this approach, the MPC and URDFIL subroutines are additionally utilized to enforce the required bounding and irreversibility inequalities on $v(\bfX,t)$ via a primal-dual active set approach. The capabilities and robustness of the proposed implementation are demonstrated by simulating the ``Nine Circles of Elastic Brittle Fracture'' on a silicate glass --- a set of tests that span the entire range of well-settled experimental knowledge on fracture nucleation and propagation. These simulations also serve to illustrate the deployment of the code using several native Abaqus finite elements, including the simplicial elements CPS3, CAX3, and C3D4.

infographic.key_insight: An Abaqus implementation combines strength-sensitive phase-field fracture with staggered displacement–damage updates and explicit enforcement of phase-field bounds and irreversibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can simulate brittle fracture nucleation and propagation using elastic properties, tensile and compressive strengths, and fracture toughness within native Abaqus elements.
method: Use UMAT and a heat-equation analogy to implement phase-field evolution with a strength-dependent driving force.
Coordinate staggered field updates through UEXTERNALDB, UAMP, MPC, and URDFIL.
Enforce phase-field bounds and irreversibility with a primal-dual active-set approach.
infographic.evidence_signal: The implementation is demonstrated on silicate glass using the “Nine Circles of Elastic Brittle Fracture” tests and native elements including CPS3, CAX3, and C3D4.
infographic.watch_item: The presented formulation targets isotropic, linear-elastic brittle materials with a Drucker–Prager strength surface; broader material applicability is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Abaqus implementation of the phase-field approach to fracture
